answer.sourceLine: Clinton delivered this line in his First Inaugural Address on 20 January 1993. The popular wording is exact — it matches the official transcript in the American Presidency Project ↗ and the Avalon Project ↗ word for word.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Our democracy must not only be the envy of the world but the engine of our own renewal. There is nothing wrong with America that cannot be cured by what is right with America. And so today, we pledge an end to the era of deadlock and drift — a new season of American renewal has begun.
trail: The official transcript at the American Presidency Project ↗ carries the exact line, spelled “cured.”
The Avalon Project ↗ at Yale Law School reproduces the same wording in its full text of the address.
Wikiquote ↗ files the line in its sourced section under the 1993 First Inaugural Address.
Project Gutenberg ↗ hosts the full address (a U.S. Government work) with the sentence intact.
source.excerptNote: The closing movement of the address. Clinton stressed the antithesis in delivery — “nothing wrong…what is right” — which is why the line became one of his most quoted.

author.metaLine: b. 1946 · 42nd President of the United States, 1993–2001 · Governor of Arkansas
author.bio: William Jefferson Clinton served two terms as the 42nd President of the United States. A former governor of Arkansas known as a fluent, improvisational speaker, he opened his presidency with a First Inaugural Address themed on “American renewal” — the speech that produced this line. He remains one of the most-quoted living American politicians.

misattribution.heading: The fine print on a genuine quote
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Clinton is correct — but three things about this line are worth getting straight.

items.why: The line is very frequently rendered “…that cannot be fixed by what is right with America.” Every authoritative transcript — the American Presidency Project ↗ and the Avalon Project ↗ — reads “cured.” Clinton himself used “cured” when he revived the line on X ↗ in 2022.

As with most presidential oratory, Clinton delivered the line but did not draft it in isolation; his chief speechwriter David Kusnet is widely credited with crafting the inaugural's language. The words are Clinton's to own as speaker, but they were written for the occasion, not spontaneous.

The “nothing wrong with America / what is right with America” antithesis echoes a stock of earlier mid-century patriotic rhetoric (a similar sentiment is often attributed to Dwight D. Eisenhower). Clinton’s specific, concise wording, however, is his own and is what entered the record in 1993.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the quote is authentically Clinton's, from the close of his 1993 First Inaugural Address — just make sure you say “cured,” per the official text ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Clinton took office in January 1993 after twelve years of Republican presidencies, campaigning on generational change and economic “renewal.” The inaugural address built toward this line as its statement of optimism — the country’s problems, it argued, would be solved by the country’s own strengths rather than by ideology or despair.

The antithesis proved durable and portable: politicians have since adapted the template to their own causes (Alaska’s Dan Sullivan and Scotland’s Alex Salmond both borrowed the ‘nothing wrong with X that can’t be cured by what’s right with X’ frame), which is part of why the line is sometimes mistaken for an anonymous proverb.
